Jacksonian physician, Oliver Wendell Holmes, had published a paper criticizing the curricula and practices of the medical schools. He thought that the apprenticeship model (with no formal education) was no longer sufficient. That was the practice in the 18th century. Jacksonian-era medicine was characterized by tremendous growth, with 1809 seeing two medical schools open and 1836 having 17 schools in operation. The industry had grown significantly faster than the corresponding academic apparatus to train the professionals and certify them.

As George Duncan Mace points out, Dionysius was not happy with the idea of the Greeks returning to Rome. However, he did at first try to help the Greeks return to their homeland. When it became clear to him that this attempt was doomed to fail, he concluded that the return to Italy was a legitimate course of action, after all, so much so that he even formed an alliance with the Italian bishop Innocent III against heretics and schismatics in the lands of the Emperor.
